rubric.why: Identifies the encoding scheme being asked about.
rubric.how: Award for identifying ASCII as the scheme.

rubric.description: Explains that ASCII lets computers or devices exchange text reliably.
rubric.how: Award for the reliable exchange of text information.

modelAnswer: ASCII enables different computers and devices to exchange text information reliably.

rubric.why: Gives the limitation of ASCII stated in the answer.
rubric.description: ASCII is limited to 7 bits and can represent 128 characters.
rubric.how: Award for both the 7-bit limit and the 128-character capacity.

rubric.why: Contrasts Unicode's capacity with ASCII's limitation.
rubric.description: Unicode can represent over a million characters through encoding forms such as UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.
rubric.how: Award for Unicode's capacity of over a million characters and its use of encoding forms.

modelAnswer: Unlike ASCII, which is limited to 7 bits and can represent only 128 characters, Unicode can represent over a million characters through different forms of encoding such as UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.

rubric.why: Identifies Unicode's role as mapping characters.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Unicode maps characters.

rubric.why: States the broad range of characters Unicode aims to map.
rubric.description: The characters are those used in the world's writing systems.
rubric.how: Award for referring to graphic characters used across the world's writing systems.

modelAnswer: Unicode is an attempt at mapping all graphic characters used in any of the world's writing systems.

rubric.why: Identifies the unsigned integer's maximum value.
rubric.how: Award for the maximum value and its 16-bit expression.

rubric.why: Identifies the minimum value in the stated range.
rubric.how: Award for stating zero as the minimum.

modelAnswer: For a 2-byte whole number (16 bits), the maximum value is 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535. The minimum value is 0.

rubric.why: Names the method used to represent negative values.
rubric.description: Negative values are stored using two's complement.

rubric.why: States the operations used to find the two's complement.
rubric.how: Award for both inverting the bits and adding 1.

modelAnswer: To store negative values, computers use two's complement: invert all the bits, then add 1 to the least significant bit (LSB).

rubric.why: States why unsigned integers suit some quantities.
rubric.description: Whole numbers often represent quantities that cannot be negative.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the quantities are non-negative.

rubric.why: States the range advantage of unsigned integers.
rubric.description: All available bits represent the value, giving a larger maximum than a same-size signed integer.
rubric.how: Award for linking use of all bits to a larger maximum value than for a signed integer of the same size.

modelAnswer: Whole numbers often represent quantities that can't be negative. Unsigned integers use all available bits for the value, so their maximum is larger than that of a same-size signed integer.

rubric.why: Explains how adding bits affects the values that can be stored.
rubric.description: More bits allow larger values to be stored.
rubric.how: Award for stating that more bits increase the range or size of values that can be represented.

rubric.why: Gives the maximum-value rule in terms of the number of bits.
rubric.description: For n bits, the maximum value is 2ⁿ − 1.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formula for the maximum value.

modelAnswer: Using more bits allows bigger values to be stored. If n is the number of bits, the maximum value is 2ⁿ − 1.
